title: Reading a Planogram: What Buyers Send You and What They Expect Back
summary: Master how to read retail planograms as spec documents and discover exactly what data buyers need back to ensure shelf compliance and sales success.
body_text: In this article, learn about: How to reframe the planogram from a simple picture to a detailed specification document The critical item data and imagery suppliers must provide to buyers to ensure a successful reset The operational consequences of inaccurate dimensions and the role of modern compliance tools For many emerging suppliers, there is a specific moment of tension that occurs right after a retailer says yes. The initial excitement of landing the account is often followed by the arrival of the complex, data-heavy planogram. If you are seeing this document for the first time, it is easy to treat it as simply a nice visual representation of where your product sits on a shelf. However, treating a planogram as a one-way document is a mistake that can lead to misplaced products, broken category flow, and lost sales. To a retailer, a planogram is a blueprint for merchandising strategy and a formal specification document. Understanding this document is important, but the relationship is a two-way street. Buyers expect you to send back accurate item dimensions, high-quality images, and specific data points to make the reset work. If you treat this exchange as optional you risk your product ending up with the wrong shelf space or facing count before it even hits the store. Decoding the Specification Document A planogram, or POG , is a schematic visual tool used to plan and control shelf layouts. It is built from sales data, shopper behavior research, and merchandising principles to ensure that products are arranged in a way to maximize space and profitability. When reviewing the planogram, it is important to look past the product images and focus on the technical instructions it contains. A complete planogram typically includes several key views that tell store teams exactly what "done" looks like. Fixture View The fixture view is the foundation of the planogram, detailing the specific equipment required, such as gondolas, pegboards, coolers, or racks. This view specifies shelf heights, depths, and the exact spacing between fixtures to ensure everything physically fits. Product View The product view layers in the specific stock keeping unit (SKU) and universal product code (UPC) data for identification. This is where you find the following: Number of facings (NoF): Tells you how many units of a product are visible from the front Number of units (NoU): Indicates the total quantity allocated to the shelf SKU Listing Finally, the document includes a SKU listing that serves as a checklist for merchandisers. This list includes barcodes , product descriptions, and units of measure to ensure the right variants are stocked. Any gap in this specification creates a decision point for a field team, and improvisation can lead to compliance errors. How To Read a Planogram Reading a planogram effectively means turning a digital schematic into a shelf that actually sells. Your goal is to ensure that the physical reality of the store matches the digital intent of the buyer. Some step-by-step best practices are: Start by identifying the fixture and shelf layout . You must confirm that the fixture type in the planogram matches the physical unit in the store. Take note of the number of shelves and their heights before any stock is placed. Once the fixture is verified, move to SKU positioning . The SKU and/or UPC from the planogram must match the actual product barcode on the carton. This prevents errors, such as stocking a 1-liter pack in a slot designated for a 500ml version. You should also count the facings on the shelf and compare them to the assigned NoF to ensure your brand blocking and visibility are maintained. Good planograms also guide category flow, showing how brands and subcategories sit next to each other to help the shopper navigate the aisle. You should verify that your products are grouped according to these brand blocks and that any specified adjacencies, like chips next to dips, are respected. If the planogram includes promotional or seasonal callouts, these must be treated as time-sensitive priorities, with end caps or dump bins set up exactly as indicated. Related Reading : Shelf Management and Planogram Optimization The Data Exchange Between You and Your Buyer While the buyer provides the layout, the accuracy of that layout depends entirely on the data you provide during the item setup process. Retailers increasingly build resets from automated item master data feeds rather than manual entry. The most critical element you owe to the buyer is accurate dimensions. This includes the height, width, and depth of the product in its final packaging. These measurements must match the actual production sample, not an estimate. If you submit inaccurate dimensions, it can throw off the automated space allocation for the entire reset. This might result in your product being given too much space, which wastes the retailer's money, or too little space, which leads to your product being left off the shelf entirely because it physically does not fit. Beyond dimensions, buyers expect high-quality product images. These images are not just for aesthetics; they allow store teams to map the correct items to the correct slots visually. Best practices for these images include using a clear white background, cropping out all borders, and ensuring the product is upright and front-facing. When working with systems like DotActiv, these images typically need to be in PNG or JPG format and named by their barcode to ensure they link correctly within the software. Major retailers like Target have a highly structured process for this data submission. Once you are selected as a vendor at Target, you have a 48-hour window to begin item setup in LaunchPad. You are responsible for completing an Item Spec Sheet, which determines which data fields you own and edit versus those the retailer manages. This data is then validated by an Item Data Specialist (IDS) to ensure everything is ready for the shelf. Related Reading : Planograms and Shelf Resets in the Beauty Aisle The High Cost of Inaccuracy Retail data is the lifeblood of a successful planogram. If your unit data is incorrect, it skews critical indicators like days of supply (DOS) and weekly movement. When DOS is miscalculated, a retailer cannot accurately balance the number of facings your product requires. Your best-selling SKU might fall behind because it wasn't allocated enough space, leading to stockouts and lost revenue. Conversely, inaccurate seasonal data could result in a shortage of products like sunscreen during its prime summer season. Inaccurate data also grinds the in-store execution process to a halt. If a field team arrives to find that the products do not fit the shelves as planned, they are forced to improvise. This often leads to reset drift, where daily restocking decisions accumulate until the shelf looks nothing like the original strategy. This unauthorized localization breaks the category logic, meaning no two stores share a consistent baseline for performance analysis. Related Reading : Why Supplier Item Data Failures Cascade and What They Cost Retailers Closing the Compliance Loop Planogram compliance means the actual store shelf matches the approved plan. Historically, many teams have overestimated their compliance because they only measured presence rather than accuracy. Today, the industry is moving toward more sophisticated verification methods. While manual checks by store staff are still common, many retailers now use photo proofing or mobile-first digital checklists to verify placement. Some are even deploying AI and image recognition tools that compare a shelf photo against the approved planogram in real-time. These systems can detect missing facings or the wrong product in a slot quickly, allowing a rep to fix the issue before they even leave the aisle. Building a Stronger Partnership Ultimately, the planogram is a tool for collaboration. While the retailer makes the final decisions, you have the opportunity to influence those decisions by providing clean data and demonstrating strong performance. In some cases, suppliers act as category leaders, providing insights on consumer behavior that help the buyer refine the category strategy. If you find that your actual packaging does not match what is reflected in a planogram, this is a signal to flag the discrepancy back to your buyer or category manager. Asking for clarification on a specific instruction is a normal part of the process and shows that you are committed to the success of the reset . By mastering the art of reading the planogram and being disciplined about the data you send back, you move from being a first-time supplier to a sophisticated retail partner. You ensure your products are positioned to win, your inventory is managed effectively, and your relationship with the buyer remains healthy. Navigating the complexities of retail execution requires a commitment to data accuracy and community knowledge. The Supply Chain Source is your destination for the expert insights and practical tools you need to lead through change. Join our community of over 60,000 professionals today to sharpen your perspective and master the evolving standards of the modern retail landscape.

title: Can One Treadmill Work for a Whole Family? | Aviron
summary: Yes, one treadmill can serve a whole family. Here is the weight capacity, user profiles and workout variety to look for, plus how the Aviron Victory compares.
body_text: Can One Treadmill Work for an Entire Family? One machine, one household. The question is whether it fits everyone who lives there. Short answer: Yes. One treadmill can serve a whole family as long as it clears three bars: a weight capacity that comfortably fits every adult (aim for 350 to 400 lb), separate profiles so each person's stats and goals stay their own, and enough workout variety that everyone actually wants their turn. The Aviron Victory Treadmill was built around all three, with a 400 lb capacity, unlimited user profiles, and a library of more than 1,000 games, classes and scenic routes. The real question is never whether a family is allowed to share a treadmill. A belt does not care who steps on it. The question is whether one machine can absorb the mismatch of a whole household: a 5 foot 2 parent who walks, a 6 foot 3 partner who runs, a teenager who wants to play something, and a grandparent who just wants twenty steady minutes. Get the wrong machine and it becomes a very expensive coat rack by month three. Get the right one and it earns its footprint every day. Here is exactly what makes one treadmill work for everyone under one roof, and how to tell before you buy. In this article Can several people really share one treadmill? What weight capacity does a family treadmill need? How many user profiles should it have? Will everyone in the house actually use it? Can kids use a treadmill safely? How do you keep a shared treadmill running well? The family treadmill checklist FAQ Can several people really share one treadmill? Yes, and most households already do it by accident. A treadmill is one of the few pieces of home fitness gear that adapts to the person, not the other way around. Speed, incline and workout length all change with a button, so the same deck that carries a brisk 3.0 mph walk in the morning can handle a 12 mph interval session at night. What separates a machine that survives a family from one that quietly breaks is not the number of users. It is two things underneath the surface. First, the physical build: can it hold the heaviest person, take double or triple the weekly mileage, and give a tall runner enough deck to stride without clipping the motor cover. Second, the software: does it keep each person's workout separate so the treadmill feels like theirs and not a shared appliance. Nail both and one treadmill comfortably covers a family of four or more. What weight capacity does a family treadmill need? Weight capacity is the first spec to check, because it is the one that fails ugly. For a single walker, 300 lb is often enough. For a family, aim higher: 350 to 400 lb. The rating is not just "can it hold me." A treadmill run near its ceiling flexes more, wears its belt and motor faster, and can void the warranty if someone tips it over the limit. Headroom is what buys you years of shared use. The Aviron Victory Treadmill is rated to 400 lb, which sits at the top of the home range and leaves margin for every adult in most households, plus the extra stress of a machine that runs several times a day instead of a few times a week. Pair that with a 3.5 CHP motor and a 20.5 inch by 57 inch deck and you have a frame built to take turns without complaint. A wider, higher-capacity deck is what lets one machine go from a morning walk to an evening run. How many user profiles should a family treadmill have? This is the spec most people forget, and it is the one that decides whether a shared treadmill feels personal or generic. Many treadmills cap you at four saved profiles. That is fine for a small family and a problem the moment a fifth person, a visiting relative or a returning college kid wants in. The Victory Treadmill supports unlimited profiles. Everyone in the house gets their own login that tracks their history, streaks, personal records and goals separately, so Dad's marathon block never muddies Mom's step count and the teenager's high score is genuinely theirs. One Aviron Family Membership covers the whole household under a single plan, and if you own more than one Aviron machine you can link them together, so the profiles and progress follow each person from the treadmill to the rower or bike. Why does this matter beyond tidiness? Because progress you can see is what keeps people coming back. A profile that remembers your streak turns "I should work out" into "I do not want to break my streak," and that small shift is the difference between a treadmill that gets used and one that gets dusted. Will everyone in the house actually use it? Here is the honest part that spec sheets skip. The reason a family treadmill fails is almost never the hardware. It is boredom. A treadmill that only offers a belt and a timer asks every family member to supply their own motivation, and most people run out of that in a few weeks. That is the motivation cliff, and it is why so much home cardio equipment ends up holding laundry. A family is the hardest possible test of this, because everyone is motivated by something different. So the machine has to offer more than one reason to step on it: The teenager wants a game with a score to beat, not a lecture about zone 2. The busy parent wants a scenic walk through Tokyo or a 20 minute guided class they do not have to think about. The runner in the house wants structured intervals and a leaderboard to race. The grandparent wants something gentle, clear and unintimidating. This is exactly what Aviron builds the machine around. Instead of one format, the Victory Treadmill runs more than 1,000 programs: games you play by walking or running, live head-to-head competition, scenic destinations, on-demand classes, streaming apps so you can watch your own shows, and guided interval workouts. The engagement is engineered into the machine rather than left to willpower, which is why 92 percent of Aviron members are still working out a year later. For a shared machine, that variety is not a luxury. It is the entire reason all four people keep using it. Different people, different reasons to step on. That is what keeps a shared treadmill in use. Built for the whole house Aviron Victory Treadmill 400 lb capacity, unlimited profiles and 1,000+ games, classes and routes, so every family member has a reason to step on. Free 30-day home trial · Financing available See the Victory Treadmill → Can kids use a treadmill safely? Yes, with rules. Aviron recommends the treadmill for ages 10 and up with adult supervision, and that guidance is a good baseline for any home treadmill. A moving belt is the single most common cause of home treadmill injuries, and children are the most at-risk group, so treat access as something you grant, not something that is always on. A few house rules keep it safe: Use the safety key or clip so the belt stops instantly if someone slips. Keep the area behind the treadmill clear, ideally with a few feet of open floor. Start slow and let younger or newer users walk before they ever jog. Store the safety key out of reach so kids cannot start the belt unsupervised. How do you keep a shared treadmill running well? More people means more miles, and more miles means maintenance matters. The good news is that a family treadmill needs the same care as any treadmill, just a little more often. Three habits cover almost everything: Check belt tension monthly. Lift the belt at its center with moderate pressure. If it rises more than about 3 inches it is too loose and can slip under a heavier or faster runner; if it barely lifts it is too tight. Adjust in small, even turns per the manual. Keep it clean. Wipe the deck and console after sweaty sessions and vacuum under and around the machine so dust does not reach the motor. With several users, do this weekly rather than monthly. Lubricate the deck on the schedule your manual lists, and sooner if the belt feels like it is dragging. Durability is also where the warranty earns its keep. The Victory Treadmill carries a 20-year warranty with an active membership, which is built for exactly this: a machine that gets used hard by more than one person, for years. The family treadmill checklist Before you buy any treadmill for a household, run it through these five questions. Here is how each one maps to what a family actually needs, and how the Victory Treadmill answers it. What to check Why it matters for a family Aviron Victory Weight capacity Must fit the heaviest adult with headroom to spare 400 lb User profiles Everyone needs their own stats, goals and streaks Unlimited Content variety Each person is motivated by something different 1,000+ games, classes and routes Deck and speed range Walkers and runners share the same deck 20.5 x 57 in deck, up to 12.5 mph Warranty Heavier shared use needs long coverage 20 years with active membership If your household leans toward more than one serious runner or you want the largest screen for classes, the Victory Treadmill Plus steps up to a 27 inch pivoting touchscreen on the same 400 lb platform. For most families, the standard Victory is the right call. If you are still deciding between a full treadmill and a compact option, our guide to walking pads versus treadmills breaks down the trade-offs, and the 12-3-30 treadmill workout is a great shared routine to start with. Frequently asked questions Is one treadmill enough for a family of four? For almost every household, yes. Treadmill sessions are short and staggered naturally across a day, so scheduling is rarely the bottleneck. The two things that make one machine enough are a high weight capacity and separate profiles, so four people can share it comfortably and still feel like it is theirs. The Aviron Victory covers both with a 400 lb rating and unlimited profiles. What weight capacity do I need for multiple users? Aim for 350 to 400 lb for a family. You are not just fitting the heaviest person; you want headroom so the belt and motor are never working near their limit, which is what keeps a shared machine durable over years of heavier-than-average use. The Victory Treadmill is rated to 400 lb. Can two people use the same treadmill back to back? Yes. Treadmills are designed for continuous use, so one person can finish and the next can start right away. If you are doing long, high-intensity sessions one after another, give the machine a short rest occasionally so the motor stays cool, and wipe the deck between users. At what age can kids use a treadmill? Aviron recommends ages 10 and up with adult supervision. Always use the safety key, keep the space behind the belt clear, and start young users at a slow walk. Store the safety key out of reach so the belt cannot be started unsupervised. Does each family member need their own membership? No. One Aviron Family Membership covers the whole household under a single plan, and every person still gets their own profile, history and goals. If you own more than one Aviron machine, you can add it to the same membership so everyone's progress carries across the treadmill, rower and bike. How long will a treadmill last with heavy family use? A well-built treadmill that is kept clean and properly tensioned will last many years even under multi-user use. The biggest factors are motor quality, weight-capacity headroom and regular maintenance. The Victory Treadmill pairs a 3.5 CHP motor and a 400 lb frame with a 20-year warranty when you keep an active membership, which is built for exactly this kind of shared, everyday use. One treadmill. Everyone in. A 400 lb frame, unlimited profiles and 1,000+ ways to move, so the whole family keeps showing up. Try it risk-free at home. body_text: View All News Valvoline Announces Pricing and Upsizing of Senior Notes Offering August 13, 2026 LEXINGTON, Ky.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Valvoline Inc. (“Valvoline”) (NYSE: VVV) announced today the pricing of its offering of $600,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 6.125% Senior Notes due 2034 (the “Notes”). The offering was upsized by $100,000,000 aggregate principal amount compared to the previously announced offering size of $500,000,000. The offering of the Notes is part of a leverage-neutral coordinated refinancing transaction intended to strengthen Valvoline’s debt maturity profile and enhance liquidity. The Notes will be unsubordinated unsecured obligations of Valvoline. Each of Valvoline’s subsidiaries that guarantees Valvoline’s obligations under its senior secured credit facilities will guarantee the Notes on an unsubordinated unsecured basis. Valvoline intends to use the net proceeds from the offering to repay in full its senior secured term loan A facility and partially repay its senior secured term loan B facility, to pay related fees and expenses, and the remainder, if any, for general corporate purposes. The offering is expected to close on August 24, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. Concurrent with the offering, Valvoline intends to enter into an amendment to its existing revolving credit facility (the “Credit Facilities Amendment”) to, among other things, increase availability thereunder from $475 million to $600 million, reduce the pricing thereof and extend its maturity to the date that is five years after the amendment effective date. The Credit Facilities Amendment is expected to enhance Valvoline’s liquidity position, reduce borrowing costs and provide additional financial flexibility. The offering of Notes is not conditioned upon the effectiveness of the Credit Facilities Amendment. The Notes will be offered to qualified institutional buyers pursuant to Rule 144A under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), and to non-U.S. persons outside the United States pursuant to Regulation S under the Securities Act. title: How to Add Your Cleva Classic Card to Your Apple Account
summary:
If you’ve ever tried to download an app, upgrade your iCloud storage, or pay for an Apple subscription through your Apple Account and realized you need a USD card, you’re not alone.

body_text: If you’ve ever tried to download an app, upgrade your iCloud storage, or pay for an Apple subscription through your Apple Account and realized you need a USD card, you’re not alone. For many Nigerians, paying for Apple services can be frustrating when your usual payment method doesn’t work. The good news is that if you have a Cleva Classic Card, you can add it to your Apple Account and use it to pay for eligible Apple services directly from your USD wallet. Important: This guide is specifically about adding your Cleva Classic Card to your Apple Account. It is not a guide to setting up your card on Apple Pay. Your Apple Account and Apple Pay are two different things. Since Apple Pay is not currently available in Nigeria, we don’t want you to confuse adding your card to your Apple Account with adding it to Apple Pay. Now, let’s get into it. What is the Cleva Classic Card? The Cleva Classic Card is a USD virtual card that lets you spend directly from your Cleva USD wallet. Unlike a traditional prepaid card, you don’t need to manually fund the card before every transaction. Once you have USD in your Cleva wallet, you can use your card for eligible online payments wherever Visa is accepted. Here are some things you can use your Cleva Classic Card for: Spend directly from your USD wallet — no card funding or funding fees. Pay at 150M+ merchants across 150+ countries wherever Visa is accepted. Pay for subscriptions such as Apple Music, Google One, ChatGPT and more. Customize your card design to make it yours. Set transaction limits to have more control over your spending. And because your card is connected to your USD wallet, you can spend your dollars without first converting them to naira. How to add your Cleva Classic Card to your Apple Account If you have a Nigerian Apple Account, you may need to make a few changes before adding your Cleva Classic Card. Follow these steps: Step 1: Change your device region to the United States On your iPhone, go to: Settings → General → Language & Region → Region Select United States as your region. Step 2: Open your Apple Account payment settings Go back to Settings and tap your name at the top of the screen. Then select: Payment & Shipping → Add Payment Method Depending on your iOS version, you may be asked to authenticate with Face ID, Touch ID or your passcode. Step 3: Enter your Cleva Classic Card details Open your Cleva app and select your Cleva Classic Card . Enter your: Card number Expiry date CVV Make sure you enter the details exactly as they appear in your Cleva app. Step 4: Enter your USD account address Apple may ask for your billing address. For this, use the bank address shown on your Cleva USD account page rather than your personal Nigerian address. You can find your USD account details in your Cleva app. Step 5: Add a phone number if requested During setup, Apple may ask you to provide a U.S. phone number. If you’re prompted for one, you can use a virtual U.S. phone number from a service such as Google Voice or another similar provider. Step 6: Save your payment method Once you’ve entered all the required information, review your details and tap Done or Save . Your Cleva Classic Card should now appear as a payment method on your Apple Account. Having trouble adding your card? First, double-check that your card details, USD account address and other information are correct. If you’re still seeing an error, take a screenshot of the message and contact Cleva Support so our team can help investigate the issue. Apple Account vs Apple Pay: What’s the difference? This is worth repeating because the two names can easily cause confusion. Your Apple Account is the account you use to access Apple’s services, purchases and subscriptions. You can add payment methods to your Apple Account to pay for things such as apps, subscriptions and iCloud storage. Apple Pay , on the other hand, is Apple’s digital wallet and contactless payment service. It lets you use supported cards to make payments in stores, online and in apps where Apple Pay is accepted. So, adding your Cleva Classic Card to your Apple Account does not mean you’ve added it to Apple Pay. And because Apple Pay isn’t currently available in Nigeria, this article focuses specifically on using your Cleva Classic Card as a payment method on your Apple Account. If you want to learn more about adding your Cleva Classic Card to Apple Pay or Google Pay, read our dedicated guide: How to Add Your Cleva Classic Card to Apple Pay or Google Pay . Why use the Cleva Classic Card? The Cleva Classic Card isn’t just useful for Apple subscriptions. It gives you a simple way to spend your USD across thousands of digital services and merchants without constantly worrying about card funding. 1. Spend directly from your USD wallet Your Cleva Classic Card connects directly to your USD wallet. So when you make an eligible transaction, the money comes directly from your available USD balance. No need to move money to a separate card balance first. And because you don’t need to fund the card before spending, you don’t have to deal with card funding fees. 2. body_text: Sphere-9 all-in-one mapping and ablation, large-tip focal, dual energy catheter first to be CE Marked for ventricular ablation New indication marks important milestone for ventricular arrhythmia patients as positive physician sentiment and global expansion for Sphere ‑ 9 continue Sphere VT U.S. pivotal trial enrollment underway GALWAY, Ireland , Aug. 6, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Medtronic (NYSE: MDT), a global leader in healthcare technology, today announced an expanded CE Mark indication for the Affera™ Mapping and Ablation System with Sphere-9™ Catheter to treat ventricular arrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia (VT) and premature ventricular complexes (PVCs). The Sphere-9 catheter is the first all-in-one mapping and ablation, large-tip focal, dual-energy catheter CE marked for ventricular ablation. "This milestone is a major step forward as we continue to expand the footprint of the Affera technology to more physicians and patients," said Rebecca Seidel, president of the Electrophysiology Therapies business at Medtronic. "Indication expansion to include ventricular arrhythmias unlocks another fast-growing market opportunity to keep building on our momentum, powered by the versatility, safety and efficiency of the Sphere-9 catheter." Additionally, in recognition of the critical unmet need for ventricular arrhythmia treatments, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted Breakthrough Device Designation for the Sphere-9 catheter for the treatment of ventricular arrhythmias, which provides an expedited regulatory pathway for the technology in this patient population. The Sphere VT pivotal trial to evaluate Sphere-9 for the treatment of VT and support future approval in the US is now enrolling patients. The Affera Mapping and Ablation System with Sphere-9 Catheter is an all-in-one, dual-energy pulsed field (PF) and radiofrequency (RF) ablation and high-definition mapping catheter for use in cardiac ablation procedures. "Physicians have long needed better tools for ventricular arrhythmias, and we're proud to deliver a technology that addresses this unmet need and moves the needle on patient care," said Khaldoun Tarakji, M.D., MPH, vice president, chief medical officer, Cardiac Ablation Solutions business, which is part of the Cardiovascular Portfolio at Medtronic. "The unique features of Sphere-9, including a single catheter to map and ablate using radiofrequency or pulsed field energy and a large footprint, make it an excellent tool for a variety of arrhythmias, including those that may be challenging to treat." About Ventricular Arrhythmias VT is a potentially life-threatening arrhythmia that causes the heart to beat abnormally fast.1 Unlike atrial fibrillation, VT affects the lower chamber of the heart and often presents after a heart attack or together with other advanced heart diseases.1,2 VT patients are often treated with medications and may receive life-saving therapies from implanted defibrillators in the form of pacing or shocks.1 Catheter ablation for VT is an established treatment option, but outcomes have remained suboptimal2 with little ablation tool innovation in recent years. As a result, a significant unmet need exists to improve patient care.3 PVCs are extra or early heartbeats that start in the heart's lower chambers (ventricles), briefly disrupting normal rhythm and potentially causing a flutter-like feeling in the chest.4 About Medtronic Bold thinking. title: How to Learn Medical Spanish: Guide for Healthcare Professionals

body_text: For healthcare professionals, a language barrier between provider and patient is more than an inconvenience. When a Spanish-speaking patient cannot clearly describe their symptoms, and a clinician cannot ask the right follow-up questions, the quality of care suffers. Medical Spanish bridges that gap, giving providers the vocabulary and conversational confidence to handle real clinical situations. Generic language courses rarely address the specific phrases, terminology, and patient interactions that come up in a healthcare setting. Focused practice on medical conversations, common diagnoses, and health-related instructions is what actually moves the needle for busy professionals. Those ready to build that skill set can learn Spanish through Parrot , a tool designed specifically for practical, real-world language use. Table of Contents Why Learning Medical Spanish Is Harder Than Learning General Spanish Why Knowing Spanish Doesn't Automatically Prepare You for Medical Conversations 7 Ways to Learn Medical Spanish 7 Best Tools to Learn Medical Spanish How to Build a Medical Spanish Learning Routine How Parrot Helps You Build Medical Spanish Through Authentic Exposure Start Learning Spanish Today Summary Medical Spanish is fundamentally different from general conversational Spanish, and treating them as the same skill is where most healthcare professionals run into trouble. A clinician who can navigate daily life in Spanish may still struggle when a patient uses informal, regional, or colloquial language to describe symptoms. That gap between social fluency and clinical communication competence is wider than most learners expect before they encounter it in practice. Self-assessed Spanish proficiency is a poor predictor of actual clinical communication ability. Research published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine found that only 13% of physicians who self-report Spanish proficiency pass a formal medical Spanish language assessment. Confidence built through general language exposure does not reliably transfer to the specific demands of a patient encounter. Communication failures, not the absence of any Spanish at all, account for the majority of medical errors involving limited English proficient patients. According to the Joint Commission, 56% of such errors are attributed to communication breakdowns. Most of those failures happen when a clinician attempts communication but lacks the clinical language depth or listening comprehension to handle the conversation accurately. Regional variation in Spanish is a significant and underestimated challenge in clinical settings. The AAMC reports more than 40 million Spanish speakers in the United States, representing communities from Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, Central America, and South America, each bringing distinct pronunciation patterns, vocabulary choices, and colloquial expressions for describing physical symptoms. Training on a single accent or standardized dialect leaves clinicians underprepared for the actual range of patients they will encounter. Vocabulary memorization alone does not build the listening comprehension that clinical Spanish requires. Patients speak quickly, use informal phrasing, change direction mid-sentence, and rely on colloquial descriptions rather than medical terminology. Developing the ability to understand real spoken Spanish across varied speakers requires consistent, repeated exposure to authentic speech, not just recognition of written terms or controlled recordings. No single tool covers every skill that medical Spanish demands. Structured courses address clinical vocabulary, audio-first tools build spoken confidence, spaced repetition apps lock in retention, and conversation practice with tutors develops spontaneous production. The most effective self-study system assigns each tool a specific role rather than relying on one approach to cover all of them. Learn Spanish addresses the listening comprehension piece specifically, using short-form video content from native speakers to build the kind of real-world auditory recognition that formal study methods typically leave underdeveloped. Why Learning Medical Spanish Is Harder Than Learning General Spanish Medical Spanish isn't a dialect—it's a completely different communication challenge entirely. General Spanish gets you through a pharmacy or hotel check-in. Medical Spanish requires you to understand what a patient means when describing pain they've never had words for , then respond with both accuracy and clarity . The gap between "I can communicate" and "I can communicate clinically" is wider than it appears . "The gap between 'I can communicate' and 'I can communicate clinically' is wider than it appears — and in a medical setting, that gap can cost lives." 🎯 Key Point: General Spanish fluency does not automatically translate into clinical competency . Medical contexts demand a higher standard of precision that requires dedicated, specialized training. ⚠️ Warning: Assuming your conversational Spanish skills are enough for patient care is one of the most dangerous mistakes a healthcare provider can make. Clinical miscommunication carries real consequences. General Spanish provides a foundation for communication, but medical Spanish requires additional vocabulary, precision, and clinical communication skills: Everyday vocabulary vs. anatomical and clinical terminology – General Spanish covers common words and phrases, while medical Spanish requires specialised language for anatomy, conditions, treatments, and care. Casual conversation flow vs. symptom elicitation and diagnosis – Everyday Spanish focuses on natural conversation, whereas medical communication requires accurately asking about and understanding symptoms. Cultural pleasantries vs. informed consent and patient safety – General conversation includes social and cultural conventions, while medical Spanish requires clear communication around consent, treatment, and patient safety. Low-stakes errors vs. high-stakes precision – Mistakes in casual conversation are usually minor, but errors in clinical communication can have serious consequences, making accuracy essential. Why vocabulary lists aren't enough Medical Spanish isn't general Spanish with extra terms added. Healthcare professionals must understand how words function in full clinical exchanges, not their isolated meanings. Knowing the Spanish word for "nausea" doesn't prepare you to ask whether it started before or after the pain, whether it comes in waves, or whether they've vomited. That requires sentence construction, contextual listening, and real-time comprehension working together. According to a 2021 survey published in PMC , while more than 80% of US medical schools offer medical Spanish education, fewer than 50% of those programs have dedicated faculty educators, leaving most training without the depth to build integrated, conversational competence. Why do patients rarely use the words you studied? The vocabulary challenge goes both ways. Patients rarely use clinical terms; they describe a burning feeling, heaviness in the chest, or pain that comes and goes. A healthcare professional trained in formal medical Spanish but not everyday conversational language will understand the textbook but miss what the patient is saying. What actually builds real communicative competence? Most professionals use printed vocabulary sheets during appointments or avoid Spanish-speaking patients and wait for interpreters. Neither builds communicative competence. What works is consistent exposure to real spoken Spanish in medical contexts: comprehensible input that trains your ear and instincts simultaneously. Parrot uses short-form video content reflecting real patient conversations rather than scripted grammar exercises, so recognition and response become automatic rather than effortful. The regional variation problem Spanish varies significantly across regions, which matters in hospitals and doctors' offices. According to the AAMC , more than 40 million Spanish speakers in the United States come from Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, Central America, and South America. Each group brings different vocabulary, regional expressions, and distinct ways of describing bodily sensations. A learner trained on one type of Spanish may understand a tutor clearly, then struggle when a patient from a different background describes the same symptom with different words. Building medical Spanish skills means training your ear to understand multiple voices, not one standard accent. This raises an important question: what happens when a Spanish speaker sits across from a clinician who thought they were ready? Why Knowing Spanish Doesn't Automatically Prepare You for Medical Conversations Conversational Spanish gets you through a dinner order or friendly exchange at the front desk. It does not get you through a patient describing chest tightness in broken sentences while visibly frightened . Those are two completely different cognitive tasks . "Conversational fluency and medical communication fluency are not the same skill — one handles social exchanges, the other handles high-stakes, life-or-death clinical moments." ⚠️ Warning: Assuming everyday Spanish fluency translates to clinical competency is one of the most dangerous misconceptions in healthcare settings — the cognitive demands are on an entirely different level. 🔑 Takeaway: Medical Spanish requires processing fear-laden , fragmented speech under pressure — a skill that casual conversational ability simply does not train you for. Conversational Spanish and medical Spanish require very different levels of precision, especially when communication happens under pressure: Everyday situations vs. clinical situations – Conversational Spanish covers things like ordering food and small talk, while medical Spanish requires describing chest tightness, pain levels, and other symptoms accurately. Low-stakes vs. high-stress communication – Everyday conversations are generally relaxed, whereas medical interactions can be high-stress and emotionally charged . Complete sentences vs. fragmented speech – Everyday speakers may use simple, complete sentences, while patients in distress may communicate in broken or fragmented speech . Social vocabulary vs. clinical terminology – General Spanish focuses on social and everyday vocabulary; medical Spanish requires clinical terminology and precise symptom language . Why does fluency still leave clinicians unprepared in the exam room? A clinician who studied Spanish for two years and traveled through Latin America can still freeze when a patient says "me pica por dentro" or "siento que me va a dar algo." Neither phrase appears in standard medical Spanish courses, yet both describe symptoms that matter. According to the Joint Commission , 56% of medical errors involving patients with limited English skills stem from communication failures: most occur not because no one tried, but because the person trying wasn't prepared for the version of Spanish that showed up in the room. What general fluency misses The pattern shows up consistently among healthcare professionals who studied Spanish seriously before starting clinical work. Someone logs hundreds of hours of input, gets comfortable with natural speech, handles daily life in Spanish without friction, and then sits across from a patient and realizes that "a basic medical intake" is not the same as confident clinical communication. General fluency builds the foundation, but the structure needed for medical conversations must be built deliberately. You need to recognize everyday symptom descriptions, not textbook terminology alone. You need to process speech under pressure, not during relaxed listening sessions. How wide is the gap between self-assessed and tested clinical Spanish? That gap is wider than most people expect. The Journal of General Internal Medicine found that only 13% of physicians who say they can speak Spanish pass a formal medical Spanish language test. What doctors believe they can do differs from what they can do when talking to patients. Why do vocabulary lists and drills fall short for real clinical listening? Most approaches to closing that gap rely on vocabulary lists, grammar drills, or structured courses. These work for recognition on paper but don't build the listening muscle needed when a patient speaks quickly, changes direction mid-sentence, or uses unfamiliar regional expressions. Platforms like Parrot use short-form video immersion built on comprehensible input, exposing learners to real spoken Spanish across different voices and contexts in sessions short enough to fit between patient appointments. The method is grounded in Dr. Stephen Krashen's research on language acquisition, which argues that fluency comes from understanding meaningful input, not from memorizing rules. The critical difference between a clinician who communicates well in Spanish and one who only thinks they do comes down to exposure and repetition across varied, real-world speech. Reading a translated symptom list is passive; hearing a nervous patient describe pain in their own words in real time is not. Build a General Spanish Foundation First Medical Spanish builds on general Spanish, not alongside it. Without common vocabulary, basic sentence structures, and question formation in place, every medical term becomes isolated. Develop everyday Spanish sufficient to ask questions, listen, and respond before adding job-specific terminology. 2. Learn High-Value Medical Vocabulary by Role Healthcare professionals need words that fit their specific role. An emergency nurse needs different terms than a physical therapist or pediatrician. Focus on words you'll use: body parts, symptom descriptions, pain scales, medication names, allergy language, and follow-up instructions. Learning deeply about relevant words is better than learning superficially about every word in a medical dictionary. 3. Learn Medical Terms Inside Real Sentences Most medical Spanish learners fail by treating vocabulary as isolated lists rather than communication tools. Knowing the word for "pain" means little without asking where it is, how long it's lasted, and whether it's changed. Practicing vocabulary within questions, dialogues, and patient scenarios gives it communicative weight. Flashcard drilling breaks down here. Most learners cycle through English-to-Spanish pairs, building recognition but not production. Apps like Parrot work differently: short-form video immersion places medical and conversational vocabulary in real spoken context, so your brain processes language through meaning rather than memorization. 4. Develop Listening Skills Across Real Speech Reading a term differs from hearing it when a nervous patient says it quickly, mid-sentence, in an unfamiliar regional accent. Listening comprehension for medical Spanish requires deliberate exposure to varied speakers, natural speech rates, and informal symptom descriptions. Educational recordings with slow pronunciation serve as a starting point, not a finish line. According to ThriveAP , over 41 million native Spanish speakers in the US bring diverse regional pronunciations, vocabulary, and communication styles into clinical settings. Training your ear on a single speaker or dialect leaves you underprepared for that range. 5. Practice Speaking Through Realistic Scenarios Medical Spanish needs to become something you can produce under pressure, not recognize in a workbook. Role-playing patient intake conversations, medication explanations , and follow-up instructions builds fluency that holds up in a real exam room. Start with predictable, structured scenarios and gradually increase spontaneity as your confidence grows. How does motivation alone fall short when a scared patient is describing symptoms? Many healthcare professionals are drawn to this work because they want to help patients in underserved communities where Spanish is the primary language. But wanting to help alone doesn't close the gap between passive Spanish knowledge and the ability to have calm, clear conversations with scared patients describing symptoms in their own words. 6. Learn Everyday and Clinical Language Together Patients rarely use clinical terminology to describe what they feel. A patient will say "me duele aquí" and point, or describe a sensation as "como hormigueo" rather than the formal term for paresthesia . Learning formal medical terms alongside the everyday Spanish patients use helps bridge the gap between classroom knowledge and clinical practice. Professionals trained only in formal medical Spanish vocabulary miss informal symptom descriptions because they lack exposure to how ordinary people describe their experiences in their own language . 7. Build Exposure to Different Spanish Varieties Spanish varies significantly by region. Patients from Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba , Guatemala, and other communities use different words, pronunciation, and regional expressions . Exposure to multiple speakers builds flexibility: you needn't learn every variety, but you should understand several. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services addresses this through its National CLAS Standards , which call for care that responds to patients' language, health literacy, cultural beliefs, and communication preferences. This is a clinical and ethical standard, not a communication preference. Put the Seven Skills Into a Weekly Routine A realistic weekly structure for a busy healthcare professional: 15–20 minutes of structured medical Spanish study on weekdays, combined with 15–30 minutes of listening. Three times weekly, practice vocabulary in sentences and short scenarios. Two to three times weekly, simulate patient interactions through role-play or conversation with a tutor. Once weekly, review challenging material and adjust accordingly. Build all seven skills in parallel rather than focusing solely on terminology. General Spanish, medical vocabulary, listening, speaking, contextual understanding, and exposure to varied speech develop together. Know the Limits of Medical Spanish Training Medical Spanish improves communication and builds rapport but does not replace qualified interpretation. The HHS CLAS Standards are clear that patients with limited English proficiency are entitled to competent language assistance, and family members or friends are not reliable substitutes in situations involving informed consent or complex medical decisions. The goal is to become a more capable, present clinician within your professional role while knowing precisely when to bring in qualified language support . Once you know what effective medical Spanish learning requires, the next question is which specific tools deliver on each of those seven skills. 7 Best Tools to Learn Medical Spanish Seven tools stand out for healthcare professionals building medical Spanish skills . Each one targets a different part of learning, creating a complete system that actually works rather than scattered study habits . "A structured, multi-tool approach to medical Spanish targets every learning layer — vocabulary, listening, speaking, and clinical application — making mastery far more achievable than isolated study." Different learning tools support different aspects of medical Spanish, so combining them can create a more complete learning routine: Vocabulary apps – Focus on medical terminology and are best for daily word retention . Audio/podcast tools – Build listening comprehension and work especially well for commute learning . Flashcard platforms – Support active recall , helping strengthen long-term memory. Video courses – Provide structured lessons that are useful for building foundational grammar . Clinical phrase guides – Focus on patient communication and help translate learning into real-world clinical situations . AI conversation tools – Provide speaking practice and support fluency building . Immersion resources – Provide full-context exposure and are particularly valuable for advanced proficiency . 💡 Tip: Don't rely on just one tool — combining at least 2–3 tools from different categories creates the strongest learning system for busy healthcare professionals. 🎯 Key Point: The real difference between professionals who achieve clinical fluency and those who plateau is using a targeted, layered approach — not random, passive exposure to Spanish content. 1. Parrot According to the PCOM Library Medical Spanish LibGuide , there are 41 million native Spanish speakers in the United States. Parrot's method is based on Dr. Stephen Krashen's research on language acquisition. Our approach closes the communication gap by having learners listen to real spoken Spanish daily rather than relying solely on grammar exercises. Short lessons, real-world content, and personalized video suggestions make Parrot ideal for healthcare workers with limited study time. 2. Canopy Canopy is built for healthcare professionals, with lessons focused on clinical vocabulary and patient communication. According to CanopyLearn Medical Spanish + LLU Health , the course includes over 40 hours of instructional material. If you work in a hospital, clinic, or urgent care setting, this offers the most direct path to role-specific medical Spanish. 3. Medical Spanish Pro Medical Spanish Pro is designed for people with existing Spanish knowledge who need to learn medical terminology for their work. It helps with patient check-in forms, discharge instructions, and symptom assessment. Rather than teaching general Spanish, it focuses on job-specific vocabulary that standard Spanish classes don't cover. 4. Duolingo Duolingo works best as a starting point, not a final destination. It builds basic sentence patterns and vocabulary through short daily sessions for beginners with little to no Spanish. The limitation is real: Duolingo teaches you to order coffee, not to ask a patient where their pain is located or whether they've had this symptom before. Use it to build momentum, then add medical-specific resources. 5. Pimsleur Most medical Spanish learners read better than they speak. Pimsleur's audio-first design forces you to listen and respond without a screen, building the pronunciation confidence and spontaneous recall that patient encounters demand. It won't teach clinical vocabulary, but it trains your ear and mouth in ways flashcard apps cannot. Why does listening practice matter more than vocabulary lists? Healthcare professionals often use vocabulary lists to learn medical Spanish quickly. But lists don't teach you to understand a patient speaking fast, nervously, and using an unfamiliar regional dialect. Parrot uses short videos from native speakers to build listening comprehension through comprehensible input—the same way people learn their first language. For busy doctors and nurses with ten minutes between shifts, regular exposure to real spoken Spanish accelerates learning beyond vocabulary cards. 6. Anki Anki earns its place in any serious medical Spanish system through spaced repetition , which shows you terms right before you're about to forget them. The key is building your own decks from words and phrases you encounter in your clinical role rather than downloading generic decks. Relevance drives retention. 7. italki Speaking practice is the most skipped yet most important step in self-directed language learning for clinical communication. italki connects you with tutors who can run simulated patient scenarios, correct pronunciation in real time, and push you to produce Spanish spontaneously rather than recognise it. Find a tutor who understands your clinical context and can structure sessions around the conversations you need to have. How these tools fit together No single tool covers every skill. Canopy or Medical Spanish Pro handles clinical vocabulary and structured medical training. Duolingo or Pimsleur builds your general Spanish foundation and spoken confidence. Anki locks in the terminology you need to retain. italki gives you the speaking practice that turns passive knowledge into active language. Parrot builds the listening comprehension that lets you understand patients when they speak, not when they answer yes or no questions. What does a strong self-study system actually look like? The strongest self-study system has each tool doing a clear job and is used consistently enough to see results. The hardest part isn't finding the right tools. It's knowing what to do first. How to Build a Medical Spanish Learning Routine Build a consistent schedule that combines medical vocabulary , general Spanish , listening , and speaking . You don't need to spend hours every day — even short, focused sessions compound into real fluency over time. Focus on communication situations that matter for your job instead of passively memorizing every medical term. "Consistency in targeted language practice — not volume — is the defining factor in clinical communication fluency." — Language Learning Research 💡 Tip: Structure your weekly routine around the 4 core pillars — vocabulary, grammar, listening, and speaking — so every session builds a different skill. A balanced learning routine combines specialised vocabulary, general language foundations, and frequent exposure to listening and speaking: Medical vocabulary – Focus on clinical terms and body systems 3× per week to build job-specific language. General Spanish – Practise grammar and sentence structure 2× per week to strengthen the underlying language foundation. Listening practice – Use patient conversations and audio daily to develop comprehension and familiarity with natural speech. Speaking practice – Practise role-play and pronunciation 2–3× per week to build confidence and active communication skills. ⚠️ Warning: Avoid the common mistake of only drilling medical terms in isolation — real clinical communication requires fluency in everyday Spanish too. 🎯 Key Point: The most effective routines prioritize job-relevant communication scenarios — like taking a patient history or explaining a diagnosis — over rote memorization of terminology. The key is to focus on communication scenarios relevant to your role rather than trying to memorize every medical term in Spanish. If You Have 30 Minutes a Day A 30-minute routine can cover the essentials 10 minutes: Study medical vocabulary and useful phrases. 10 minutes: Listen to medical or general Spanish. 5 minutes: Review vocabulary you've encountered in context. 5 minutes: Practice speaking, shadowing, or self-talk. For example, if you're preparing to work with Spanish-speaking patients in a clinical setting, your vocabulary practice could focus on symptoms and medical history while your listening practice exposes you to people describing health problems naturally. If You Have 60 Minutes a Day With an hour available, increase your exposure and speaking time rather than simply adding more vocabulary memorization: 15 minutes: Structured medical Spanish study. 20 minutes: Medical or authentic Spanish listening. 10 minutes: Contextual vocabulary review . 15 minutes: Speaking, role-play, or conversation. This gives you enough time to work on both specialized medical language and the broader Spanish skills needed to communicate naturally. Build Your Week Around Real Communication Your daily schedule doesn't need to look identical. A weekly routine can help you maintain variety while making sure you're practicing the skills that matter. Every day: Get some exposure to both general Spanish and medical Spanish. 3–4 times a week: Include focused listening or shadowing. 2–3 times a week: Review medical vocabulary you've encountered in context. 1–2 times a week: Practice role-play or conversation with a tutor, language partner, or colleague. Once a week: Complete a longer scenario-based practice session and identify the areas where you struggled. Practice Scenarios You Actually Encounter Don't try to learn medical Spanish as one enormous subject. Start with situations you're likely to encounter in your work. You could practice Taking a medical history. Asking a patient about their symptoms. Discussing pain and its severity. Asking about medications and allergies. Explaining preparation for a procedure. Giving basic follow-up instructions. Communicating with a patient's family members. For each scenario, learn the vocabulary you need, listen to examples of the language being used, and then practice producing your own questions and responses. This is more practical than memorizing hundreds of medical terms without knowing when or how you'll use them. Combine Medical Spanish With General Spanish It's also important not to let medical terminology completely replace general Spanish practice . A patient may talk about their health, but they may also explain what they were doing when their symptoms began, describe their daily routine, discuss their family, or ask questions about their appointment. General Spanish gives you the foundation for those conversations, while medical Spanish gives you the specialized vocabulary needed to discuss healthcare. Your routine should therefore include both. Know When Medical Spanish Isn't Enough Learning medical Spanish can improve your ability to communicate with Spanish-speaking patients, but it does not replace qualified medical interpretation when professional interpretation is required. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services states that covered healthcare organizations must take reasonable steps to provide meaningful access for people with limited English proficiency and identifies competent oral interpretation as an important form of language assistance. Your language-learning routine should therefore complement your organization's interpreter policies and established clinical communication procedures. When a situation requires a qualified interpreter, use one rather than relying on your personal Spanish ability. Make Authentic Spanish Part of the Routine A structured medical Spanish course can teach you the terminology and phrases you need, but you also need to hear Spanish being used naturally. That means making room for understandable, authentic Spanish alongside your medical study. Regular exposure can help you become more comfortable with different voices, speaking speeds, accents, everyday vocabulary, and the way Spanish sounds outside a textbook. For independent learners, that's often one of the hardest parts of maintaining a medical Spanish routine: finding enough Spanish you can understand and engage with outside your structured medical lessons. And that's where the right learning environment can help you continue developing your listening skills beyond the medical vocabulary you're deliberately studying. How Parrot Helps You Build Medical Spanish Through Authentic Exposure Medical Spanish training teaches you essential medical words and phrases, but you need to get comfortable hearing and processing Spanish as people actually use it . Parrot supports this by providing real, easy-to-understand Spanish content that works seamlessly with structured medical Spanish study . "You need to get comfortable hearing and processing Spanish as people use it, not memorizing vocabulary in isolation." — Core Principle of Authentic Language Acquisition 💡 Tip: Don't rely on structured drills alone . Authentic exposure to real Spanish speech bridges the gap between classroom knowledge and real-world fluency . 🔑 Takeaway: Parrot combines comprehensible input with medical Spanish study , giving you structured learning and authentic language exposure in one place. What happens when medical Spanish lessons focus too much on terminology? The problem You can memorize medical vocabulary without becoming comfortable understanding Spanish when people speak it in real time. Knowing the Spanish word for a symptom doesn't mean you'll recognize it when someone mentions it naturally in conversation. How Parrot helps Our platform uses comprehensible input through engaging short-form videos to expose you to real Spanish from native speakers. Learners hear Spanish in complete sentences and real conversational contexts rather than studying isolated words. The outcome You strengthen general listening comprehension alongside structured medical Spanish training, becoming more comfortable understanding Spanish beyond vocabulary exercises. How does Parrot make authentic Spanish accessible when it feels too difficult? The problem Native Spanish content can be valuable, but it isn't always easy to access for learners still building their listening skills. Fast conversations that are difficult to understand can be frustrating. How Parrot helps Our AI-powered recommendation feed personalizes Spanish videos based on your skill level and interests, eliminating the need to search through content that's too easy or too difficult. The outcome You gradually increase listening practice difficulty as your understanding improves, rather than struggling with advanced native content from the start. How does Parrot help when unfamiliar vocabulary interrupts your listening? The problem When you encounter unfamiliar words, you must stop watching and look them up in a dictionary, which disrupts your comprehension of the overall message. body_text: News Details View All News Capri Holdings Limited Announces First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Results August 5, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Revenue, Operating Income and Earnings Per Share Exceed Expectations LONDON--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Capri Holdings Limited (NYSE:CPRI), a global fashion luxury group, today announced its financial results for the first quarter of Fiscal 2027 ended June 27, 2026. First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Highlights from Continuing Operations Revenue decreased 3.5% on a reported basis and 4.1% in constant currency Operating margin was 2.2%; adjusted operating margin was 3.6% Earnings per share were $0.60; adjusted earnings per share were $0.67 John D. Idol, the Company's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, said, "We are encouraged by our first quarter results, which exceeded our expectations and demonstrated the progress we are making to build a stronger and more profitable business. Our strategic initiatives across both Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo are driving deeper consumer engagement through enhanced brand storytelling and compelling product innovation." Mr. Idol continued, "As we look at the balance of fiscal 2027 we expect Jimmy Choo to continue to grow and return to profitability. At Michael Kors certain headwinds including lower than anticipated inventory levels in the second quarter, softer trends in EMEA and updated foreign currency exchange rate assumptions are impacting our revenue outlook. As a result we now expect fiscal 2027 revenue of approximately $3.4 billion. Based on our revised revenue expectations we are taking actions to reduce operating expenses which are enabling us to maintain our fiscal 2027 earnings per share outlook of approximately $2.15, representing 40% growth over the prior year." Mr. Idol concluded, "Looking beyond fiscal 2027 the opportunity for Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo remains significant. As our strategic initiatives continue to gain momentum, Capri Holdings is well positioned to drive sustainable growth, enhance profitability and create meaningful long-term value for our shareholders." First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Results Financial Results and Non-GAAP Reconciliation The Company's results are reported in this press release in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States ("U.S. GAAP") and on an adjusted, non-GAAP basis. A reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP financial information is provided at the end of this press release. As previously disclosed, on April 10, 2025, the Company and Prada S.p.A. (“Prada”) entered into a Stock Purchase Agreement (the “Purchase Agreement”) whereby Prada agreed to acquire certain subsidiaries of the Company which operate the Company’s Versace business. As a result, the Company classified the results of operations and cash flows of its Versace business as discontinued operations in its consolidated financial statements for all periods presented. The related assets and liabilities associated with the discontinued operations were classified as held for sale in the consolidated balance sheets as of June 28, 2025. On December 2, 2025, the Company completed the sale of its Versace business. Unless otherwise noted, the discussion below, including analysis of financial condition and results of operations, relates only to continuing operations. Overview of Capri Holdings First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Results Total revenue of $769 million decreased 3.5% compared to last year. On a constant currency basis, total revenue decreased 4.1%. Gross profit was $500 million and gross margin was 65.0%, compared to $502 million and 63.0% in the prior year. The 200 basis point increase in gross margin was primarily driven by higher full-price sell-throughs and lower tariff rates relative to the first quarter of fiscal 2026. Income from operations was $17 million and operating margin was 2.2%, compared to income from operations of $16 million and operating margin of 2.0% in the prior year. Adjusted income from operations was $28 million and adjusted operating margin was 3.6%, compared to $20 million and 2.5% in the prior year. Net income was $69 million, or $0.60 per diluted share, compared to net income of $56 million, or $0.47 per diluted share, in the prior year. Adjusted net income was $76 million, or $0.67 per diluted share, compared to $60 million, or $0.50 per diluted share, in the prior year. Net inventory as of June 27, 2026 was $624 million, a 20% decrease compared to the prior year. Cash flow provided by operating activities for the first quarter was $73 million, while capital expenditures were $25 million, resulting in free cash flow of $48 million. Cash and cash equivalents totaled $114 million, and total borrowings outstanding were $338 million, resulting in net debt of $224 million as of June 27, 2026 versus $1.5 billion as of June 28, 2025. Michael Kors First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Results Michael Kors revenue of $590 million decreased 7.1% compared to last year. On a constant currency basis, Michael Kors revenue declined 7.6%. Approximately $10 million of revenue was attributable to earlier than anticipated timing of wholesale shipments. Michael Kors gross profit was $377 million and gross margin was 63.9%, compared to $388 million and 61.1% in the prior year. The 280 basis point increase in gross margin was primarily driven by higher full-price sell-throughs and lower tariff rates relative to the first quarter of fiscal 2026. Michael Kors operating income was $55 million and operating margin was 9.3%, compared to $63 million and 9.9% in the prior year. The 60 basis point decline in operating margin was primarily due to expense deleverage on lower revenue. Jimmy Choo First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Results Jimmy Choo revenue of $179 million increased 10.5% compared to last year. On a constant currency basis, Jimmy Choo revenue increased 9.3%. Jimmy Choo gross profit was $123 million and gross margin was 68.7%, compared to $114 million and 70.4% in the prior year. The 170 basis point decrease in gross margin was primarily driven by channel mix. Jimmy Choo operating income was $13 million and operating margin was 7.3%, compared to operating income of $4 million and operating margin of 2.5% in the prior year. The 480 basis point increase in operating margin was primarily due to expense leverage on higher revenue. Share Repurchase Program During the fiscal first quarter, the Company spent $50 million to repurchase approximately 2.6 million ordinary shares in open market transactions at an average cost of approximately $19.31 per share. As of June 27, 2026 the remaining availability under the Company's share repurchase program was $871 million. Outlook The following guidance is provided on an adjusted, non-GAAP basis. Guidance assumes an incremental 10% tariff rate on imports into the United States through July 24, 2026 and 10% to 12.5% thereafter. Financial results could differ materially from the current outlook due to a number of external events which are not reflected in our guidance, including changes in global macroeconomic conditions, incremental tariff rates in excess of our assumptions, greater than anticipated inflationary pressures or weakening consumer confidence, and further considerable fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates. Fiscal Year 2027 Outlook For Capri Holdings, the Company now expects the following: Total revenue of approximately $3.4 billion impacted by approximately $50 million from lower than anticipated second quarter revenue at Michael Kors due to inventory delays, $50 million from softer trends in EMEA due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and $35 million from foreign currency headwinds relative to our prior expectation. Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures Constant currency effects are non-GAAP financial measures, which are provided to supplement our reported operating results to facilitate comparisons of our operating results and trends in our business, excluding the effects of foreign currency rate fluctuations. Because we are a global company, foreign currency exchange rates may have a significant effect on our reported results. The Company believes presenting metrics on a constant currency basis will help investors to understand the effect of significant year-over-year foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations and provide a framework to assess how the business is performing and expected to perform excluding these effects. We calculate constant currency measures and the related foreign currency impacts by translating the current year's reported amounts into comparable amounts using prior year's foreign exchange rates for each currency. All constant currency performance measures discussed in this press release should be considered a supplement to and not in lieu of our operating performance measures calculated in accordance with U.S. GAAP. The Company also presents free cash flow, which is a non-GAAP measure and is calculated by taking net cash provided by operating activities less capital expenditures for the period. The Company believes that free cash flow is an important liquidity measure of cash that is available after giving effect to our capital and strategic plans, and that it is useful to investors because it measures the Company’s ability to generate cash. Additionally, this earnings release includes certain non-GAAP financial measures that exclude certain one-time, non-recurring costs associated with restructuring activities, our store renovation plan, merger and divestiture transactions and Capri transformation initiatives. The Company uses non-GAAP financial measures, among other things, to evaluate its operating performance and in order to represent the manner in which the Company conducts and views its business. The Company believes that excluding these items, which are not comparable from period to period, helps investors compare operating and financial performance in a manner consistent with management's evaluation of ongoing business performance. While the Company considers the non-GAAP measures to be useful supplemental measures in analyzing its results, they are not intended to replace, nor act as a substitute for, any amounts presented in its consolidated financial statements prepared in conformity with U.S. GAAP and may be different from non-GAAP measures reported by other companies. Our strength lies in the unique DNA and heritage of each of our brands, the diversity and passion of our people and our dedication to the clients and communities we serve. title: Deli Meal Recall: Kroger, Publix and Other Stores Affected Across Three States
summary: Consumers in several states are being urged to check their refrigerators and freezers after federal food safety officials announced a recall involving thousands of pounds of prepared deli meals.
